## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Aṭṭhamakakathā* (Kv 3.5) is a debate found in the third chapter of the *Kathāvatthu*, the fifth book of the Theravāda *Abhidhamma Piṭaka*. The discussion centers on the status of the "eighth person" (*aṭṭhamaka* or Sanskrit *aṣṭamaka*), who is defined across Buddhist doctrinal literature as a practitioner striving on the first stage of the noble path toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala-sacchikiriyāya paṭipanna*) [La Vallée Poussin 1991; Jones 1949; Gethin 2001]. Specifically, the debate examines whether the eradication of active manifest defilements or outbursts (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), such as wrong views (*diṭṭhi*), adherence to rules and rituals (*sīlabbata*), and doubt (*vicikicchā*), at this preparatory path stage necessarily entails the eradication of their underlying dormant dispositions (*anusaya*) [Dutt 1978; Waldron 2003]. According to the Kathāvatthu commentary, rival schools such as the Andhakas and the Sammitīyas maintained a distinction between active defilements and latent tendencies, asserting that an *aṭṭhamaka* may discard the former without instantly abandoning the latter, thereby remaining separated from the fruit of stream-entry for a significant time; the Theravādin interlocutor opposes this division, treating the suppression of outbursts as inextricably linked to the cessation of their latent dispositions [Dutt 1978; Waldron 2003].
